name: Adaiah
title: Father of Jedidah and a name borne by several biblical figures
summary: Adaja is a Hebrew personal name meaning 'Yahweh has adorned', and it is borne by several different individuals in the Old Testament. The most prominent among these is Adaja of Boskat in the lowlands of Judah, father of Jedidah, who became the mother of the reforming king Josiah of Judah. Through this connection, Adaja played an indirect but significant role in the Davidic royal line and in Judah's religious renewal under Josiah. Other bearers of the name include a Levite from Asaph's lineage associated with temple music, a priest named Adaja son of Jeroham who served in Jerusalem after returning from the Babylonian exile, as well as two men who were commanded to send away their foreign wives during Ezra's reforms. The fact that the name appears over a span of several centuries, from the time of the divided kingdom through the post-exilic period, testifies to its enduring popularity as an expression of trust in Yahweh's goodness and care.

keyEvents.title: Adaiah as father of Jedidah
keyEvents.description: Adaiah from Boskath is mentioned as the father of Jedidah, who became the mother of the godly King Josiah of Judah. Through his daughter, Adaiah had an indirect connection to the Davidic royal line and to Josiah's important religious reforms.

keyEvents.title: Adaiah among the Levitical families
keyEvents.description: An Adaiah is mentioned among the Levites in the genealogies of Chronicles, linked to the lineage of Asaph and the Levitical service at the temple.

keyEvents.title: Adaiah as a priest in Jerusalem after the exile
keyEvents.description: A priest named Adaiah, son of Jeroham, is mentioned among the priests who settled in Jerusalem after returning from the Babylonian exile, with the task of serving in the rebuilt temple.

keyEvents.title: Adaiah as a Priest in the Books of Chronicles
keyEvents.description: In 1 Chronicles, Adaiah, son of Jeroham, is listed as one of the priests who served in Jerusalem. This is likely the same person mentioned in Nehemiah's parallel list.

keyEvents.title: Adaiah Among Those Who Had Taken Foreign Wives
keyEvents.description: During Ezra's time, two men named Adaiah are mentioned among those who had taken foreign wives and were required to send them away as part of Ezra's religious reforms to preserve the people's loyalty to Yahweh.

versions.summary: Adaiah is a name that appears in several places in the Old Testament and refers to different individuals. The most well-known Adaiah was the father of Maaseiah and the grandfather of Jedidah, mother of King Josiah, as well as a Levite from the tribe of Judah. The name means 'Yahweh has adorned' or 'Yahweh has decorated.'
versions.title: Levitical Ancestor and Priest
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Levitical ancestor and priest' is somewhat misleading since the profile concerns several different individuals named Adaja, not only Levites/priests. A broader title would have been more accurate.; [major] Since the profile covers multiple persons named Adaja from various time periods (divided kingdom, exile, return), it is misleading to list only 'divided-kingdom'. The most prominent Adaja (grandfather of Jedidah) belongs to the divided kingdom period, but others belong to the return era. For a composite profile, one should choose the era of the central figure, but this should be made clear.; [minor] The lifespan 'ca. 800–700 BC' fits Adaja as the grandfather of Jedidah (mother of Josiah), but the profile gathers several persons, so this may be confusing. Josiah reigned ca. 640–609 BC, and his mother Jedidah was the daughter of Adaja from Boskat (2 Kings 22:1). The grandfather relationship to Jedidah is uncertain – the text states that Jedidah was 'daughter of Adaja', not daughter of Maaseiah. The timeframe should be adjusted.; [major] The summary says that Adaja was 'father of Maaseiah and grandfather of King Josiah's mother Jedidah'. But according to 2 Kings 22:1, Jedidah was 'daughter of Adaja from Boskat' – thus Adaja was Jedidah's father, not her grandfather. Maaseiah is not mentioned in this context. The text apparently mixes two different persons/relationships.; [major] The father is given as 'Ethan', but this does not fit the best-known Adaja. In 1 Chronicles 6:41 an Ethan is mentioned in the Levitical genealogy, but the connection to this specific Adaja is uncertain. For Adaja the priest (Nehemiah 11:12; 1 Chronicles 9:12), the father is Jeroham. Family relationships should be clarified based on which Adaja is the primary focus.; [major] The child is listed as 'Maaseiah', but 2 Kings 22:1 states that Jedidah was the daughter of Adaja – thus it is Jedidah, not Maaseiah, who is the child of the Adaja connected to Josiah's lineage. Maaseiah is not mentioned in the Bible as a child of this Adaja.; [minor] The roles include only 'priest', but the profile describes several Adajas with different roles. Some were priests, one was an ancestor of the queen mother Jedidah, and another is mentioned in connection with taking a foreign wife. 'Ancestor' or 'Levite' could be added.; [major] The event states that Adaja was 'grandfather of Jedidah', but 2 Kings 22:1 says that Jedidah was 'daughter of Adaja from Boskat'. Thus Adaja was Jedidah's father, not her grandfather. The description must be corrected.; [minor] The verse reference Ezra 10:29,39 lists verses 29 and 39 as separate verses. There are actually two different Adajas in Ezra 10 – one in verse 29 (among the sons of Bani) and one in verse 39 (among the sons of Shimei). It may be worth clarifying this, and the formatting should show that these are two separate occurrences.

footnotes.text: The name Adaiah (Hebrew: עֲדָיָה, ʿĂdāyāh) means 'Yahweh has adorned' or 'Yahweh has decorated.' It is composed of the root עדה (ʿādāh, 'to adorn/decorate') and the theophoric element יה (Yah, a short form of YHWH). Theophoric names with the Yah/Yah-element were very common in ancient Israel and Judah, testifying to a strong tradition of expressing trust in God through naming.

Adaiah of Boskath is mentioned as the father of Jedidah, mother of King Josiah (2 Kings 22:1). Boskath (Hebrew: בָּצְקַת) was a city in the lowlands of Judah (Shephelah), mentioned in Joshua 15:39. Archaeologically, the area has been identified with Tell el-Baṣṣi, southeast of Lachish, placing this Adaiah in the core region of the southern kingdom of Judah.

Several individuals named Adaiah appear in the biblical writings, which was common for theophoric names in Israel. The fact that the name appears across different time periods—from the era of the divided kingdom to after the Babylonian exile—shows its enduring popularity as an expression of faith in Yahweh's favor and care.

In Nehemiah 11:12 and 1 Chronicles 9:12, a priest named Adaiah, son of Jeroham, is mentioned. These two texts contain parallel genealogical lists for priests who served in Jerusalem after returning from Babylon. Such lists were crucial for confirming the legitimacy of the priestly line in the rebuilt temple worship.

In Ezra 10:29 and 10:39, two different men named Adaiah are mentioned among those who had taken foreign wives. Ezra's reforms were motivated by fear of religious syncretism, and the requirement to separate from non-Israelite wives reflects a strict interpretation of the Torah's prohibition against intermarriage with Canaanite peoples.

The Levitical Adaiah mentioned in 1 Chronicles 6 is linked to the lineage of Asaph. Asaph was one of the leading temple musicians under King David, and his descendants played a prominent role in temple music and liturgical tradition over several generations.

In rabbinic tradition, King Josiah was highlighted as one of the most godly kings in Judah's history. The fact that his mother's family background is specifically mentioned in the text—with her father Adaiah from Bozkath—suggests that the piety of his mother and her family was considered a contributing factor to Josiah's character and willingness to reform.
